claims.old: ### 11.1 No shared mutable model: staged writes, snapshot reads
claims.new: ### 11.1 No shared mutable model: staged writes, snapshot reads

claims.old: Everything in the periphery (GUI, input devices, network I/O, logging) runs on tasks the loop does not control, and every one of them wants the data the loop is stepping.
claims.new: Everything in the periphery (GUI, input devices, network I/O, logging) runs on tasks the loop does not control, and every one of them wants the data the loop is stepping.

claims.old: FlightCore's answer is one big lock.
claims.new: FlightCore's answer is one big lock.

claims.old: `SimControl` and the live `Model` are guarded by `io_lock`, with one task per attached interface reading or mutating the model under it (sim.jl).
claims.new: In FlightCore's `sim.jl`, `SimControl` and the live `Model` are guarded by `io_lock`, with one task per attached interface reading or mutating the model under it.

claims.old: That lock does enforce the boundary-visibility rule (§10.3), because it is only ever free between steps.
claims.new: That lock does enforce the boundary-visibility rule (§10.3), because the lock is only ever free between steps.

claims.old: Transplanting it here was nevertheless rejected, on three structural costs (D-022). One of the three is decisive for everything below.
claims.new: Transplanting the lock here was nevertheless rejected, on three structural costs (D-022). One of the three is decisive for everything below.

claims.old: Under a lock, input timing is scheduler-determined and unrecorded.
claims.new: Under a lock, input timing is scheduler-determined and unrecorded.

claims.old: There is then no defined input trace, and bit-identical replay (§10.7) is unachievable in principle for interactive runs.
claims.new: There is then no defined input trace (the primary record of a session), and bit-identical replay (the ordinary loop with its drain reading the trace, §12.7) is unachievable in principle for interactive runs.

claims.old: The replacement has five planes.
claims.new: The replacement has five planes.

claims.old: Its unit of account is the frame (one iteration of the loop: drain, integrate, boundary sequence, publication), the grid step §10.1 names.
claims.new: The replacement's unit of account is the frame (one grid step, §10.1).

claims.old: (one iteration of the loop: drain, integrate, boundary sequence, publication)
claims.new: Each frame is one iteration of the loop, which runs the drain (the frame-top swap that applies staged device writes to the root inputs), then integrates, then runs the boundary sequence, then publishes.

claims.old: A frame is what `step!` counts, and it is the ordinal that keys the trace.
claims.new: A frame is what `step!` counts, and it is the ordinal that keys the trace (D-101).

claims.old: "Per frame" means this throughout the document.
claims.new: "Per frame" means this throughout the document.

claims.old: The kinematic reference frames of the aircraft domain are a different word, and they always appear compounded: the b frame, the ECEF frame.
claims.new: The kinematic reference frames of the aircraft domain are a different word, and they always appear compounded, as in the b frame and the ECEF frame.

claims.old: 1. Staging (inbound). Devices submit pending input writes at any wall-clock moment, never touching live root inputs (§11.4).
claims.new: 1. Staging is the inbound path (§11.4). Devices (attached participants in the periphery) submit pending input writes at any wall-clock moment, never touching live root inputs (the root component's own input faces).

claims.old: 2. The drain. Exactly one point in each frame, at its top, where the loop takes the staged batches and applies them to the root inputs.
claims.new: 2. The drain is exactly one point in each frame, at its top, where the loop takes the staged batches (each device's set of pending writes) and applies them to the root inputs (D-022).

claims.old: It never happens at a `t` boundary (§10.4).
claims.new: It never happens at a `t` boundary (§10.4).

claims.old: Between drains the loop owns its data exclusively, and no lock is held during stepping, ever.
claims.new: Between drains the loop owns its data exclusively, and no lock is held during stepping, ever.

claims.old: 3. Publication (outbound). At the end of each boundary sequence the loop publishes an immutable snapshot.
claims.new: 3. Publication is the outbound path. The loop publishes an immutable snapshot (a boundary-consistent signal table with its framework status) at the end of each boundary sequence (D-022).

claims.old: Readers observe it without coordinating with the loop (§11.2).
claims.new: Readers observe it without coordinating with the loop (§11.2).

claims.old: 4. Control. Pause, pace and stop live on a separate few-word atomic surface (§12.1).
claims.new: 4. Control places pause, pace and stop on a separate few-word atomic surface (§12.1, D-022).

claims.old: 5. Task topology. One loop on the calling task, one spawned task per rostered device, all run-scoped.
claims.new: 5. Task topology places one loop on the calling task (the task that invoked `run!`) and one spawned task per rostered device, all run-scoped.

claims.old: The fifth plane carries the most machinery, and the rest of this section spells it out.
claims.new: The fifth plane carries the most machinery, and the paragraphs below spell it out.

claims.old: Device tasks are run-scoped.
claims.new: Device tasks are run-scoped (D-093).

claims.old: `run!` spawns one task per roster entry after device `init!`, and §12.4 joins them all at every stop (§12.6).
claims.new: `run!` spawns one task per entry of the roster (the list of attached device entries) after device `init!`, and §12.4 joins them all at every stop (§12.6).

claims.old: `attach!` never spawns.
claims.new: `attach!` never spawns.

claims.old: It registers, in a stopped-sim state only (§11.3), and the task appears at the next `run!`.
claims.new: It registers, in a stopped-sim state only (§11.3), and the task appears at the next `run!`.

claims.old: The loop runs on the calling task (D-310).
claims.new: The loop runs on the calling task (D-310).

claims.new: A task exists only once the run it serves exists.

claims.new: Any first-boundary synchronization a device needs is the counter-plus-condition predicate wait (§12.3), never a `Base.Event` latch.
